issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may not rely on a later inquiry into alleged fraud to set aside a consent decree when the same allegation was previously rejected after the debtor failed to produce evidence and the appellate court did not follow the procedure for receiving additional evidence.
material_facts: The judgment debtors alleged in execution proceedings that the consent decree had been obtained by fraud but did not lead evidence or make substantive submissions to support the allegation.
The executing court rejected the fraud objection by a reasoned order, which was not promptly challenged.
Years later, the appellate court directed a subordinate court to inquire into the fraud allegation and relied on its report to set aside the decree.
The appellate court did not follow the prescribed process for admitting additional evidence.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court erred in obtaining and relying on the later report, which gave the judgment debtors an opportunity to fill the evidentiary gap, and its finding that the decree was obtained by fraud could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Fraud must be pleaded and established by evidence; a bare allegation is insufficient. Under Order XLI Rules 27, 28 and 29 of the Code of Civil Procedure, additional evidence may be received only when the required conditions and procedure are followed. The appellate court cannot direct evidence-taking outside that procedure to remedy a party’s failure to prove its case earlier.

predicates.appeal_challenges_consent_decree: A party appeals against a consent decree on the ground that it was obtained by fraud.
predicates.fraud_objection_previously_rejected: A court has already rejected the party’s fraud objection in the proceedings enforcing the decree.
predicates.debtor_failed_to_produce_evidence_on_obj: The party alleging fraud did not produce evidence to substantiate that allegation when it was first considered.
predicates.appellate_court_relied_on_later_inquiry_: An appellate court obtains and relies on a later inquiry into the fraud allegation without following the required procedure for receiving additional evidence.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a consent decree for fraud, the allegation was already rejected after the party failed to prove it, and the appellate court relies on a later inquiry obtained without the proper additional-evidence process, that later finding cannot support setting aside the decree.

issues.legal_issue: A court should not set aside an unchallenged rejection of a fraud objection after the execution sale has been confirmed and a sale certificate has been issued.
material_facts: The judgment debtors did not promptly challenge the executing court’s order rejecting their fraud objection.
The property was sold in execution, the sale was confirmed, and a sale certificate was issued and registered before the judgment debtors challenged the earlier order.
The appellate court later set aside the earlier order rejecting the objection.
issues.conclusion: The appellate court could not properly set aside the earlier order after the sale had been confirmed and the sale certificate issued; its decision setting aside that order could not be sustained.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order XXI Rules 92 and 94 of the Code of Civil Procedure, when the relevant applications to set aside an execution sale are disallowed, the sale is confirmed and becomes absolute, and a sale certificate is then issued. The Court treated the sale’s confirmation and issuance of the certificate as final in the circumstances of this case.

predicates.execution_proceeding: The dispute arises in proceedings to enforce a court decree.
predicates.fraud_objection_order_left_unchallenged: The party alleging fraud did not challenge the order rejecting that objection before the execution sale was completed.
predicates.execution_sale_confirmed_and_certificate: The court confirmed the execution sale and issued a certificate to the purchaser.

issues.definition: In enforcement proceedings, when the rejection of a fraud objection remains unchallenged until the execution sale is confirmed and a certificate is issued, the earlier rejection should not be set aside.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal may be maintained to contest whether a compromise should have been recorded in a decree.
material_facts: The judgment debtors appealed against a decree recorded on the basis of a compromise.
The appeal contested whether the compromise should have been recorded.
issues.conclusion: The appeal against the consent decree was maintainable.
issues.legal_principle: Although Section 96(3) of the Code of Civil Procedure bars an appeal against a decree passed with the parties’ consent and Order XXIII Rule 3A bars a separate suit to set aside a decree on the ground that its compromise was unlawful, Order XLIII Rule 1A(2) permits an appellant in an appeal against a decree in a suit recording a compromise to contest whether the compromise should have been recorded. The Court relied on Banwari Lal v. Chando Devi, AIR 1993 SC 1139.

predicates.appeal_from_consent_decree: A party brings an appeal against a decree recorded on the basis of a compromise.
predicates.appeal_contests_whether_compromise_shoul: The appeal challenges whether the court should have recorded the compromise.

issues.definition: An appeal from a consent decree is maintainable when it contests whether the compromise should have been recorded.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to an execution sale cannot succeed on grounds outside the sale-related case advanced in the application, and the application was rightly dismissed where the judgment debtors did not make the deposit required by the court or allege fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale.
material_facts: The judgment debtors applied to set aside the execution sale, alleging inadequate publication to obtain an adequate market value and alleging fraud in obtaining the decree.
They did not allege fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale, and their principal fraud allegation concerned the decree itself.
They did not deposit the sale consideration with interest as required by the executing court.
The appellate court set aside the dismissal by relying on the purchaser’s relationship to the judgment creditor, a ground not advanced in the sale application.
issues.conclusion: The executing court rightly dismissed the application to set aside the sale, and the appellate court erred in reversing that dismissal on a ground not raised in the application.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure permits an application to set aside an execution sale on the ground of material irregularity or fraud in publishing or conducting the sale. The Court also upheld the executing court’s application of the deposit requirement it attributed to that rule and held that the appellate court had gone beyond the case advanced in the application.

predicates.application_to_set_aside_execution_sale: A party applies to set aside a sale conducted to enforce a court decree.
predicates.no_required_deposit_made: The applicant fails to make the deposit that the court requires for the sale challenge.
predicates.alleged_fraud_concerns_decree_not_sale: The applicant alleges fraud in obtaining the decree rather than fraud or material irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale.
predicates.appellate_court_relied_on_ground_not_rai: The appellate court reverses the dismissal by relying on a ground that the applicant did not advance in the application.

issues.definition: When a party challenges an execution sale, fails to make the required deposit or alleges fraud only in obtaining the decree, and the appellate court relies on an unpleaded ground to reverse dismissal, the dismissal should stand.
